Quick answer: Non-surgical treatments are the first line of defence for most people with arthritis, aiming to reduce pain and improve joint function. These often include specific exercises, pain management strategies, and medication, which can significantly improve quality of life. Doctors usually recommend trying various non-surgical options for several months before discussing surgery. Surgery often manages symptoms rather than providing a complete cure.

Overview

A patient-friendly decision framework.

What the evidence shows

UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Versus Arthritis consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus.

What this means for you

  • Talk to your clinician. Personalised advice always beats blanket rules.
  • Track your symptoms. Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days.
  • Move within comfort. Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood.
  • Watch the warning signs. New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review.

Practical next steps

  1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: related guidance.
  2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment.
  3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day.

Editorial standards

This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis Editorial Team and reviewed by our Clinical Review Board against UK NICE guidance and peer-reviewed sources. We update content at least annually.

What the Evidence Says

Large-scale studies, including randomised trials and systematic reviews, consistently show that non-surgical treatments are the first line of defence for most people living with arthritis. These treatments, which include specific exercises, pain management strategies, and medication, aim to reduce pain, improve joint function, and slow disease progression. For many, these approaches are highly effective and can significantly improve quality of life, often delaying or even avoiding the need for surgery.

Clinical guidelines from professional bodies across the UK reinforce this staged approach. They recommend a comprehensive assessment of all non-surgical options before considering surgical interventions. This is because surgery, while sometimes necessary and highly effective, carries risks and requires a significant recovery period, which may not be suitable or beneficial for everyone.

The evidence also highlights the importance of individualised care. What works for one person may not work for another, even with similar conditions. Shared decision-making, where patients and clinicians discuss all available options, their potential benefits, and risks, is a cornerstone of effective arthritis management according to current evidence.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Ignoring early symptoms: Hoping pain will disappear often leads to more advanced problems. *Fix: Discuss new or worsening symptoms with your GP promptly. Overdoing it on good days: Pushing through significant pain can cause flare-ups and damage. *Fix: Adjust activity levels based on your energy and pain, even if you feel well. Stopping medication too soon: Discontinuing prescribed drugs without advice can worsen your condition. *Fix: Always consult your doctor before changing your medication regimen. Relying solely on surgery for a 'cure': Surgery often manages symptoms rather than curing the underlying condition. *Fix: Understand that post-surgical rehabilitation and ongoing self-management are crucial. Not asking enough questions: Feeling rushed or unsure about your treatment plan. *Fix: Prepare questions in advance and don't hesitate to ask for clarity.

When to Speak to a Clinician

While routine check-ups are important, certain changes or symptoms warrant a more urgent discussion with your GP, physiotherapist, or rheumatologist. Early intervention can often prevent more serious issues and help manage your condition more effectively.

  • Sudden, severe pain in a joint.
  • New, unexpected swelling or redness around a joint.
  • Fever alongside joint pain or swelling.
  • Rapid or unexplained loss of joint function or an inability to bear weight.
  • Symptoms that are significantly worsening despite your current treatment plan.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long should I try non-surgical treatments before considering surgery?

There isn't a one-size-fits-all answer, as it depends on your specific condition, symptoms, and how you respond to treatment. Your doctor will typically recommend trying a range of non-surgical options for several months, often longer, before discussing surgery.

Will surgery cure my arthritis completely?

In most cases, surgery for arthritis aims to relieve pain, improve function, and correct deformities, rather than providing a complete cure. Arthritis is a chronic condition, and even after surgery, ongoing management and lifestyle adjustments are usually necessary.

What should I expect during the recovery period after arthritis surgery?

Recovery varies greatly depending on the type of surgery and your overall health. You can expect a period of rehabilitation involving physiotherapy and pain management, often lasting several weeks to months. Your healthcare team will provide a detailed recovery plan tailored to your needs.

Practical next steps for Expert Q&A: How Do I Know If Surgery Is Right for Me?

If you came here about Expert Q&A: How Do I Know If Surgery Is Right for Me?, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask community musculoskeletal services about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Working with NHS pathways

Most people start with GP care, community physiotherapy and self-management, with rheumatology involved when inflammatory disease is suspected or treatment needs escalate. Ask what monitoring blood tests or reviews you should expect, and who to contact between appointments if a flare escalates.

Everyday eating patterns

No single food cures arthritis. Patterns rich in vegetables, fruit, pulses, wholegrains and oily fish are the ones most often discussed in UK dietetic advice for inflammatory conditions. Keep changes realistic: swap one ultra-processed snack for fruit and nuts, or cook with olive oil more often than seed oils marketed as miracle cures.

Quick questions about Expert Know Surgery Right

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.
